top_cluster.headline: The House passed a Russia sanctions bill and sent it to Trump while Speaker Johnson recessed the chamber early, sidelining Rep. Thomas Massie's push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and a House vote to release more Epstein files.
top_cluster.left_framing: Left and far-left outlets (Mother Jones, Guardian, PBS) frame Johnson's recess as a fear-driven, deliberate cover-up protecting Hegseth from accountability for an 'unauthorized' Iran war, paired with blocking Epstein file releases — emphasizing executive overreach, GOP complicity, and institutional evasion of oversight.
top_cluster.center_framing: Center outlets (Axios, The Hill, NPR) treat the Johnson-Massie recess fight as a notable political/procedural story — Axios explicitly frames it as leadership dodging accountability votes — while covering the Russia sanctions bill's bipartisan-but-uneasy passage and new executive authority with relatively neutral, process-focused language.
top_cluster.right_framing: Right and far-right outlets (Fox, Breitbart) center Massie's own accusation that Johnson is protecting Hegseth, treating it largely as an intra-Republican procedural drama and factional dispute rather than a substantive accountability failure; broader right coverage otherwise emphasizes the Russia sanctions bill as a Trump tariff-power win and downplays Democratic reluctance as vindication.
top_cluster.left_omissions: Left coverage largely omits Massie's own conservative/libertarian rationale for the impeachment push (limiting executive war powers) and doesn't engage with right-leaning framing that treats this primarily as an intra-GOP squabble rather than a bipartisan accountability failure.
top_cluster.right_omissions: Right coverage (aside from Fox's Massie piece) largely omits the Epstein-files-release angle tied to the same recess, and downplays or ignores the argument that the recess timing was a deliberate shield for Hegseth, instead framing it through Massie's individual grievance.

blindspot_narrative: The left is avoiding the AI industrial-policy fight almost entirely, despite heavy Democratic-aligned tech-donor exposure, while amplifying Trump-adjacent conflict-of-interest and accountability stories (Kushner's business dealings, DOGE's $9.5bn no-work payments, the Israel arms sale holdout). The right is avoiding direct scrutiny of Hegseth's Iran conduct and the DHS free-speech overreach against Streever — both stories that would normally appeal to civil-liberties or accountability instincts on the right — while flooding coverage with culture-war opinion content and AI-deregulation advocacy. Both patterns suggest each side is protecting its coalition's most exposed flank: the left's tech-donor class, the right's executive-branch loyalty.
